P·17  ·  MOBILITY  ·  ON THE VF BUILD SLATE

FuelITThe cheapest litre, on your actual route.

Any fuel app can point at a cheap station. None we know of does the real arithmetic: the litres a detour burns against the cents it saves, what your tank can reach, what a fill costs your car. FuelIT solves the whole equation, then hands the wheel to the navigator you already trust.

WHY IT HAS TO EXIST

Fuel apps show you prices.
Nobody does the maths.

Pump prices are one of the last honest arbitrage games left for ordinary people: the same litre can differ by twenty cents across one town in one day. The tools built for it stop at a coloured map pin.

F·01

Cheap is not cheapest

The lowest price on the map can be the most expensive stop on your trip: twelve kilometres of detour can burn more fuel than the discount saves. The full equation (detour litres burned versus cents saved, per candidate station) is the entire point, and no mainstream app we know of computes it.

F·02

Crowdsourced and stale

Most fuel apps run on driver-reported prices, hours old and sometimes wildly wrong. Official feeds exist: German law requires stations to report every price change within five minutes, France publishes every station's price on a ten-minute cycle, Spain and Austria run open government APIs. The good data is public. The apps mostly aren't built on it.

F·03

You are the product

The dominant fuel apps are ad businesses, and some have been reported to collect and sell driver location data to third parties. A consumer-protection test in Germany rated multiple fuel-price apps critical on data protection. An app that knows every route you drive should not be in the data business.

F·04

Your car is a stranger

Price-per-litre is half a number. The EU already requires stations to display fuel cost per 100 km, because that is the real figure. No app knows your tank size, your consumption or how much fuel you're carrying right now, so none can say what's reachable, or what this fill costs your car.

ONE STATION'S PRICE SWINGS ~10 CENTS IN A SINGLE DAY. THE WINDOW IS REAL
WHO IT SERVES

Built for everyone
who pays the lazy price.

Our own tanks first

The VF network drives in two very different fuel markets. At home in Malta, pump prices are state-stabilised: one flat price nationwide, no game to play. On the network's German roads the same litre swings by around ten cents a day at a single station. FuelIT proves itself the VF way, on our own fills and real German price cycles, before any customer touches it. If it can't beat our own fuel bill, it doesn't ship.

NOIRDA GMBH · DEVF EMPIRE CORP · MTOFFICIAL FEEDS ONLY

Commuters

You drive the same roads every day, and there is a documented cheap window most evenings. FuelIT learns your loop, watches the cycle and tells you when today's fill is worth it and when to wait until tomorrow.

Long-haul & holiday drivers

On cross-border trips the price logic changes at the border. FuelIT reads several national feeds along one route and gives one answer: where to stop, in which country, before the motorway prices get you.

Vans, trades & small fleets

Fuel sits among a small firm's top costs, and no one has time to shop for it. Per-vehicle profiles and route-aware stops handle the fuel line on the P&L for you.

Every powertrain, eventually

Charging prices are a wilder market than petrol ever was: tariff jungles, roaming cards, per-minute traps. The same route mathematics applies. FuelIT covers combustion first and charging next.

WHAT IT CHANGES

From map pins
to a decided stop.

The measure of a fuel app is whether the stop it picks was the cheapest one for your car, your route and your tank. We judge FuelIT on the euros left in your account.

The whole equation.

FuelIT solves detour distance, fuel burned to get there, litres you'll take and price you'll pay for each candidate station, then ranks them by the true cost of the stop.

Official numbers.

Built on government price feeds: five-minute-fresh by law in Germany, ten-minute cycles in France, open ministry APIs in Spain and Austria. No crowd guesses, no hours-old pins.

Your routes stay yours.

An app that sees every drive you make must never be a data business. FuelIT processes routes and location to answer your question and sells them to no one. The architecture enforces this; there is no settings toggle.

THE MECHANICS

Four layers,
one decision.

Built the VF way: deterministic mathematics doing the ranking, official data underneath, and a clean handoff at the end. FuelIT decides the stop; your favourite navigator drives you there. Like every VF system, it leaves the lab with the engine fitted and the harness tuned.

LAYER 1

Feed engine

One live price lattice normalised from official national sources: Germany's transparency unit feed, France's open-data flux, Spain's ministry API, Austria's regulator service, Italy's price observatory. Each country is an adapter; the lattice is one.

LAYER 2

The vehicle twin

You register your car once and FuelIT pulls its full data: tank size, real consumption, fuel type. From there it computes live range from the fuel you're carrying, true €/100 km per station, and a hard gate on which stops are reachable at all.

LAYER 3

Route mathematics

FuelIT scores each candidate station on and near your route on the full detour equation (extra kilometres, litres burned, litres taken, cents saved) plus the documented intraday price cycle. Sometimes the best answer is "wait two hours."

LAYER 4

The car link

We designed FuelIT to pair with the GPS navigator in your car. Select your route and every petrol station along it appears in sequence with its live price; the chosen stop then deep-links into Google Maps, Waze or your in-dash navigation. FuelIT does the deciding, your navigator does the driving.

QUESTIONS

Asked.
Answered.

Which countries does FuelIT cover?

R·01 covers nine countries: Germany, France, Spain, Italy, Austria, the UK, Portugal, Malta and Luxembourg, each with its official price feed integrated. On cross-border trips FuelIT reads several national feeds along one route and gives one answer: where to stop, and in which country. The Netherlands and Belgium follow as two more country adapters in R·03.

Where do the prices come from?

Official government feeds, never crowdsourced pins. German law requires stations to report every price change within five minutes, France publishes every station's price on a ten-minute cycle, Spain and Austria run open government APIs, and Italy's price observatory completes the set. FuelIT normalises them into one live price lattice, with each country as an adapter.

Does FuelIT replace the navigator in my car?

FuelIT decides the stop and your navigator drives you there. Select a route and every station along it appears in sequence with its live price. R·01 ships with NAV·IT, VF's own turn-by-turn, so your route never touches Google or Apple maps. From R·02 the chosen stop can also hand off to Google Maps, Waze or your in-dash navigation if you prefer.

What does FuelIT cost?

The Core tier is free forever: live prices on your route, station cards and the full map. Plus is €9.99 a year (€0.83 a month) and covers the thinking: range maths, automatic handoffs, price-drop alerts, CarPlay and Android Auto. The price you join at is the price you renew at. These are planned launch figures; VF confirms them at each release.

Does FuelIT sell my location or my routes?

No. An app that sees every drive you make must never be a data business. FuelIT processes routes and location to answer your question and sells them to no one; the architecture enforces this and there is no settings toggle. The published privacy model sets out what VF retains (nothing joinable to you) and what third parties see (nothing).

Does FuelIT work for electric cars?

FuelIT covers combustion first and charging next. Charging prices are a wilder market than petrol ever was, with tariff jungles, roaming cards and per-minute traps, and the same route mathematics applies. R·03 points the detour equation at charging tariffs using ChargePlace and NAP data, alongside an opt-in, k≥50-anonymised traffic layer for NAV·IT and two more country adapters.
